questions.question: A Splunk SOC analyst pulls a search returning many duplicate events that share the same `src_ip` + `dest_port`. They want ONE event PER unique (src_ip, dest_port) pair (keep the first). Which SPL command does this?
options: `deduplicate` — NOT a real Splunk SPL command; unlike `dedup`, there is no `deduplicate dest_port` form in SPL
`unique` — NOT a real Splunk SPL command; unlike `dedup`, there is no `unique dest_port` form in SPL
`dedup src_ip, dest_port`
`distinct` — NOT a real Splunk SPL command; unlike `dedup`, there is no `distinct dest_port` form in SPL
questions.explanation: The `dedup` command removes duplicate events that share the same value for a specified field. For example, `dedup src_ip` keeps only the first event for each unique source IP. You can use `dedup N fieldname` to keep the first N events per unique value.

questions.question: A Splunk admin counts events per host with `index=main | stats count by host`. What does this exact pipeline return?
options: Total number of events in the index — false; would be `stats count` without `by`
Number of unique hosts — false; that would be `stats dc(host)` or `stats values(host) | stats count`
List of all hosts with their field values — false; that would be `table host *`
A count of events GROUPED BY the host field
questions.explanation: The `stats count by host` command is a transforming command that returns a table with each unique value of `host` and the count of events that have that value. The `by` clause specifies the field(s) to group by.

questions.question: A Splunk SPL search must match events where `status` is 404 OR 500 (both are valid HTTP error codes the SOC is investigating). Which forms are valid SPL syntax?
options: `status=(404 OR 500)` is one of the valid forms with correct syntax to match events — VALID; parenthesised boolean with a single field reference works
All three of these forms are valid SPL syntax to match `status` = 404 or 500
`status=404 OR status=500` is NOT one of the valid forms; this syntax does not match events correctly when sharing a field name — false; this is a valid boolean OR form that correctly matches events
`status IN (404, 500)` is NOT one of the valid forms; its syntax does not match events in Splunk SPL — false; the `IN` clause is valid since Splunk 6.5+ as a shorthand
questions.explanation: All three syntaxes are valid in Splunk SPL. The `IN` operator (introduced in Splunk 6.3) is a shorthand for multiple OR conditions on the same field. `status IN (404, 500)` is equivalent to `status=404 OR status=500` and also to `status=(404 OR 500)`.

questions.question: After a search, an analyst wants the result column `src_ip` to display as `SourceIP` (purely a rename of the result column, no data change). Which SPL command?
options: `| alias src_ip=SourceIP` — `alias` is not an SPL renaming command
`| fields src_ip AS SourceIP` — `fields` selects columns; doesn't rename
`| rename src_ip AS SourceIP`
`| eval SourceIP=src_ip | fields - src_ip` — works as a side-effect but is more verbose than `rename`
questions.explanation: The `rename` command renames a field. `rename src_ip AS SourceIP` (the AS keyword is case-insensitive) renames the field in the results. Note that after renaming, you must use the new name in subsequent pipeline commands. The `eval` + `fields` approach also works but is less clean.

questions.question: An SPL search computes a NEW result-column at query time: `... | eval response_kb = response_bytes / 1024`. Which describes the `eval` command's purpose in Splunk?
options: Filters events matching a condition — false; that's `where` (which uses eval-style expressions but is filter, not column-creator)
Evaluates dashboard panel expressions at display time — false; that's the dashboard XML / Studio renderer
Runs external scripts against results — false; that's `script` or custom search commands
Calculates / creates new fields, or modifies existing field values, using expressions (math, string, boolean)
questions.explanation: The `eval` command calculates an expression and puts the resulting value into a new or existing field. For example, `eval total_mb = bytes / 1048576` creates a `total_mb` field. `eval` supports mathematical, string, boolean, and comparison operators as well as dozens of built-in functions.

questions.question: An analyst runs a search with `earliest=??? latest=now`. The required earliest is 'the BEGINNING (00:00:00) of the current day'. Splunk's time-modifier syntax uses `@` to snap to the START of a unit. Which `earliest` value?
options: `earliest=-1d` — 24 hours ago (rolling), NOT the start of today
`earliest=now/d` — not Splunk's syntax (that's Elasticsearch's)
`earliest=0d` — NOT valid; no '0d' form in Splunk time modifiers
`earliest=@d`
questions.explanation: In Splunk relative time modifiers, the `@` character snaps to the nearest time unit boundary. `earliest=@d` means 'snap back to the start of the current day (midnight)'. Similarly, `earliest=-7d@d` means '7 days ago, snapped back to midnight of that day'.

questions.question: A Splunk analyst is choosing between `chart` and `timechart` for time-series aggregation. The key difference: ONE automatically uses `_time` as the X-axis and creates time bins (defaulting based on the search time range); the other lets the analyst pick any field as the X-axis. Which describes `timechart`?
options: `timechart` supports more aggregation functions and automatically computes extended bins on any axis field — false; chart and timechart share the same function set
`timechart` is faster because it automatically creates fewer intermediate results by locking the axis to `_time` — false; performance is comparable for equivalent queries
`timechart` automatically uses `_time` as the X-axis and creates time-bucket bins (span), while `chart` requires an explicit X-axis field
`timechart` only creates line charts and automatically chooses the best bin granularity for any axis field — false; it works with multiple visualisation types; span must be specified
questions.explanation: The `timechart` command is a specialized version of `chart` where `_time` is always the X-axis (split-by column). It automatically creates time buckets based on the search time range. `chart` requires you to specify both X and Y axes. Both are transforming commands.

questions.question: An analyst wants the TOP-10 most common values of the `user_agent` field along with their count + relative-frequency percent. Which SPL command produces this in one line?
options: `topvalues user_agent` — not a real SPL command
`stats top(user_agent)` — not the correct syntax (no `top()` stats function)
`top user_agent`
`rare user_agent` — returns LEAST-common values, the OPPOSITE of what's needed
questions.explanation: The `top` command returns the most common values of a field with count and percentage columns. By default it shows 10 results. Use `top limit=N field` to change the limit. The `rare` command does the opposite — it shows the least common values.

questions.question: Splunk search has THREE modes: (Fast) disables field discovery, only `_raw` and default fields are populated; fastest. (Smart) field discovery happens only if needed (default); balance of speed + features. (Verbose) all fields discovered + all event-time transforms applied; slowest, richest. Which describes Fast vs Smart vs Verbose?
options: Fast = no field discovery / no rendering, max speed
Fast limits field discovery on indexers / Smart limits field discovery on search heads / Verbose limits field discovery on heavy forwarders — false; modes affect WHAT'S COMPUTED, not WHERE
Differ only in pagination speed — false; they differ in whether field discovery and event rendering are performed
Verbose builds a knowledge base of field discovery rules from all matching events — false; lookups + extractions are configured separately in props.conf and transforms.conf
questions.explanation: Splunk search modes: **Fast** disables field discovery and event rendering for maximum performance; **Verbose** builds all fields, event types, and tags (slowest but most complete); **Smart** (default) switches behavior based on whether the search uses transforming commands — if so, it acts like Fast; if not, it acts like Verbose. Smart auto-selects based on command type

questions.question: An SPL analyst needs to PARAMETERISE a search using the result of another search. For instance: 'find all events with src_ip in the list returned by a separate search for failed-login source IPs'. Splunk supports embedding one search inside another. Which describes the syntax and semantics?
options: Subsearch runs AFTER the main search — false; it runs FIRST (the outer search uses the subsearch result)
A subsearch is enclosed in square brackets and its RESULTS are passed as arguments to
Subsearch in a new tab — false; subsearch is inline
Saved search reference — that's `loadjob`, not subsearch syntax
questions.explanation: A subsearch is a search within a search, enclosed in square brackets `[...]`. It runs first and its results are passed to the outer search as filter criteria. For example: `index=main [search index=threat_intel | fields src_ip]` finds events where src_ip matches any value in the threat_intel index. By default, subsearches have a 60-second timeout and return max 10,000 results.

questions.question: A Splunk SPL search needs to add a new field that holds the CHARACTER LENGTH of the `url` string field from each event. The team plans `... | eval url_length = ???(url)`. Which Splunk eval function returns the character count of a string?
options: `length(field)` — NOT a Splunk eval function (that's PHP / Java's `length()`); Splunk eval doesn't expose `length()`
`strlen(field)` — NOT a Splunk eval function (that's C); Splunk eval doesn't expose `strlen()`
`len(field)` — the Splunk eval string-length function; returns the number of characters
`count(field)` — `count` is a stats function (counts events), not an eval string-length function
questions.explanation: Splunk SPL's eval string-length function is `len(X)` (e.g. `eval url_length = len(url)`). There is no `length()` or `strlen()` in Splunk eval. `count()` is a stats aggregator, not a string function. PRIOR VERSION marked `length()` as correct, which is factually wrong — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An analyst wants to EXTRACT a field `user` from raw event text containing `user=alice@example.com`. They use the `rex` command at search time with a named-capture regex. Which Splunk SPL syntax is correct?
options: `rex field_extract user="user=.*"` — wrong: no `field_extract` parameter in `rex`
`rex "user=(?P<user>[^\s]+)"` — wrong: that's Python-style named capture; Splunk uses `(?<name>...)` without the P
`rex extract user from "user=<user>"` — wrong: not Splunk SPL syntax
`rex field=_raw "user=(?<user>[^\s]+)"`
questions.explanation: The `rex` command uses regular expressions with named capture groups in the format `(?<fieldname>regex)` to extract fields. `rex field=_raw "user=(?<user>[^\s]+)"` extracts everything after 'user=' up to the first whitespace into a field called `user`. The `field=_raw` parameter tells `rex` which field to match against (default is `_raw`).

questions.question: An admin sets up an alert: 'fire when the COUNT of failed logins from a single IP exceeds 10 in any rolling 15-minute window'. The Splunk alert condition selector lets them pick the trigger type. Which option fits?
options: Number of events > 10 — refers to raw event count, not the aggregated `stats count by src_ip` result rows
Number of results > 10
Custom condition: `count > 10` — works but rendered as 'Number of Results' in the UI
Number of hosts > 10 — counts distinct hosts, wrong dimension here (IPs)
questions.explanation: For a stats-based search like `stats count by src_ip | where count > 10`, the alert trigger 'Number of results > 0' fires when any row passes the `where` filter. If using a raw event count without stats, use 'Number of events > 10'. The key distinction: 'results' counts rows in a table, 'events' counts raw events in a non-transforming search.

questions.question: An analyst wants to ENRICH search results with data from an external CSV (`asset_owners.csv`) — joining on a key field. The CSV is loaded as a Splunk knowledge object that can be referenced in searches. Plus a SPL command lets you load the CSV contents directly into the search pipeline (no event correlation, just rows). Which describes Splunk lookups + `inputlookup`?
options: Lookups enrich events with data from external CSV/KV/Geo sources, joining on a key field
Lookups map index names to labels using an external reference table; `inputlookup` lists all defined lookups and can enrich events by index label — wrong; lookups are not index-label maps
Lookups are field-alias tables that enrich events by joining on external alias mappings; `inputlookup` shows those mappings — wrong; field aliases are a separate knowledge object
Lookups are saved searches that enrich results by joining on external criteria at schedule time; `inputlookup` runs them on demand — wrong; saved searches and lookups are distinct objects
questions.explanation: A Splunk lookup enriches events with additional fields by matching a lookup key field to rows in an external CSV or KV store. The `lookup` command performs this enrichment mid-search. The `inputlookup` command reads the entire lookup table as a search result set, useful for inspecting or joining lookup data directly. inputlookup reads the lookup file as a search source

questions.question: Splunk supports AUTOMATIC LOOKUPS: a lookup configured in `Settings → Lookups → Automatic lookups` so it's applied to EVERY search against a specified host / source / sourcetype WITHOUT requiring `| lookup …` in the SPL. Which describes this?
options: A lookup that is configured as a scheduled saved search and automatically applied to enrich results on each scheduled run — that is a saved-search + outputlookup combination, not automatic lookup

A lookup configured with an auto-refresh interval in Settings that periodically re-reads the CSV and applies updated values to future searches — that describes KV Store collection refresh, not automatic lookup
A lookup configured in Settings → Lookups → Automatic Lookups that is automatically applied to search results when an event contains the lookup's input field
A lookup that is automatically applied when writing new entries, auto-creating records for each unique field value encountered — lookups are read-only by default and do not auto-write
questions.explanation: An automatic lookup (configured in Settings > Lookups > Automatic Lookups) is applied automatically at search time whenever events contain the lookup's input field — without requiring `| lookup` in the search string. This is useful for enriching events at index time or universally, such as automatically adding hostname from IP using a DNS lookup table.

questions.question: In Splunk's `stats` command, two functions both aggregate the unique values of a field into a list. (A) Returns a SET (deduplicated, sorted). (B) Returns a LIST (keeps duplicates, preserves order). Which is `values()` vs `list()`?
options: `values(field)` deduplicates + sorts
`values` sorts the field results alphabetically; `list` preserves event order but does not dedup — partial; the key distinction is deduplication, not just ordering
`list` deduplicates the field results; `values` keeps all entries including duplicates — REVERSED; this is the opposite of actual behavior
`values` and `list` produce identical field results — false; they differ in deduplication and ordering behavior
questions.explanation: `values(field)` returns a multivalue field with the distinct (deduplicated) values for the grouped events, sorted lexicographically. `list(field)` returns all values in the order they appear, including duplicates. Use `values()` when you want unique entries; use `list()` when ordering or duplicates matter.

questions.question: A search `index=web | stats avg(bytes) AS avg_bytes BY status` returns a row `status=200 avg_bytes=15234`. What does that row mean?
options: Status 200 occurred 15234 times/min — wrong; avg is computed across bytes not time
The AVERAGE response size in bytes for status=200 was 15234 bytes
15234 events had status=200 — that would be `count` not `avg(bytes)`
15234 = median bytes — wrong; avg ≠ median
questions.explanation: The `avg()` statistical function in `stats` calculates the arithmetic mean of the specified field. Combined with `by status`, it groups events by the status field and computes the average `bytes` for each group. A result of 15,234 for status=200 means HTTP 200 responses averaged 15,234 bytes in size.

questions.question: An analyst wants to SAMPLE only the FIRST 20 events from a search (in returned order, before any sort). Which SPL command?
options: `first 20` — not a real SPL command
`head 20`
`limit 20` — not a real Splunk SPL command (that's SQL-style)
`top 20` — returns the top 20 BY FREQUENCY of a field, not first-in-pipeline
questions.explanation: The `head` command returns the first N events from a search. `head 20` returns the first 20 events. The `tail` command returns the last N events. `top` is a transforming command that finds the most common values of a field — unrelated to limiting results to N events.

questions.question: An admin wants `clientip` to be queryable as ANOTHER name (e.g. `src_ip`) so legacy dashboards using `src_ip` continue to work without changing the data. Splunk supports defining `src_ip → clientip` as a search-time mapping. Both names refer to the same underlying field. Which Splunk knowledge object is this?
options: Placeholder created by eval — different mechanism (eval creates a new field by computing an expression, not by aliasing)
Nickname for a saved search — wrong concept; a saved search alias does not create an alternate field name
Field alias
Index nickname — different concept (Splunk does not expose a field alias at the index level)
questions.explanation: A field alias creates an alternative name for an existing field. Both the original and alias names can be used interchangeably in searches. Field aliases are configured in Settings > Fields > Field Aliases and are applied per source type. They are useful for normalizing field names across different data sources (e.g., aliasing `src` to `src_ip` across various source types).

questions.question: An analyst writes an SPL pipeline `index=web | stats dc(user_agent)` against a busy web index. The intent is to surface a single number summarising how many DISTINCT user-agent strings appeared in the search window. What does `dc()` do in this context?
options: `dc(field)`
`dc(field)` — sums numeric values of `field`; would be wrong because user_agent is a string and there is nothing to add
`dc(field)` — averages numeric values of `field`; unrelated to counting distinct strings
`dc(field)` — concatenates all values into a single multi-value string; not a counting function
questions.explanation: `dc(field)` (short for `distinct_count(field)`) counts the number of unique values in a field across the grouped events. For example, `stats dc(src_ip) as unique_IPs by dest_port` tells you how many unique source IPs connected to each destination port. This is different from `count()` which counts total events.

questions.question: A SOC wants to CATEGORISE events at search time without modifying the raw data. They define a SEARCH expression (e.g. `index=fw action=blocked` → category 'firewall_deny'). Any event matching the search inherits the category tag. Which Splunk knowledge object?
options: Lookup — different (external file enrichment that adds fields; does not categorise events by search expression)
Event type
Field alias — different (renames existing fields; does not categorise events by search expression)
Tag — applies to field VALUES, not to the event search expression used for categorisation
questions.explanation: An event type is a search expression saved as a knowledge object that categorizes events based on field-value pairs or search terms. Events matching an event type get an `eventtype` field with the event type's name. Tags can then be applied to event types. Event types are useful for grouping similar events across data sources.

questions.question: Splunk has two related knowledge objects. (A) TAGS — apply to specific field=value pairs (e.g., `host=web01` gets tag `production`). (B) EVENT TYPES — defined by a SEARCH expression; events matching the search inherit the event-type label. Tags can be APPLIED to event types as well. Which describes tags vs event types?
options: Tags = result-only metadata labels with no search impact; event types = system-defined categories — false; both are user-defined search-time objects
Tags = metadata labels visible only in the UI; event types = applied at index-time — false; both are search-time knowledge objects that do not alter the index
Tags = metadata labels on raw events only; event types = applied to indexed fields — false; tags apply to specific field=value pairs, not raw text
Tags = metadata labels applied to field VALUES
questions.explanation: A tag is a label applied to a specific field=value pair (e.g., tag the value 'sshd' in the 'process' field as 'authentication'). Tags are searched using `tag=<tagname>`. An event type is a categorization saved as a search — events matching the search get tagged with the event type name. Both help normalize and categorize data, and work well together. Tags are searched with tag=<value>

questions.question: A reusable SPL fragment `failed_logins` takes ONE argument (the index name). When called as `\`failed_logins(security)\``, it should expand to `index=security action=failure`. Splunk's macro syntax uses `$arg$` for argument substitution inside the macro definition. Which definition?
options: `index={index} action=failure` arg-count 1 — `{}` is not Splunk macro syntax; the argument placeholder must use `$` delimiters
`index=$index$ action=failure` with argument count = 1
`index=$$index$$ action=failure` with 0 args — wrong: 0 args means no argument placeholder is recognised in the macro definition
`index=%index%` arg-count 1 — `%%` isn't Splunk macro syntax; argument substitution requires `$arg$` delimiters
questions.explanation: Splunk search macros use `$argument_name$` syntax for arguments. The macro definition would contain `index=$index$ action=failure`, and you'd set the argument count to 1. The macro is invoked with backtick syntax: `` `failed_logins(main)` `` which expands to `index=main action=failure`. Argument names must match between the definition and the invocation.

questions.question: An SPL `chart count BY status OVER host` produces a 2-D matrix. What role does the field specified by the `over` clause play in the resulting table?
options: It sets the display threshold table cutoff above which additional series are grouped into an 'OTHER' bucket — that is the `limit` option, not the `over` clause
It restricts the time range for the chart table output, filtering rows to events within that field's value range — time filtering uses `earliest`/`latest`, not the `over` clause
It specifies the field used as the X-axis (rows in the table), with one row per unique field value
It sets the maximum number of series to display in the chart table — that is controlled by `limit`, not by the `over` clause
questions.explanation: In the `chart` command, the `over` clause defines the X-axis (the row field). The `by` clause defines the column series. For example, `chart count over host by status` creates a table where each row is a host, each column is a status code, and each cell contains the count. The `over` and `by` clauses together define the two dimensions of the chart.

questions.question: Two filtering primitives in SPL: (A) `search` — appears at the START of pipelines and after pipes; uses keyword + field=value matches; FAST because it can use indexed fields. (B) `where` — appears after pipes; uses eval-style boolean expressions like `where bytes > 1000 AND http_method="POST"`. Which describes `where` and the difference?
options: `where` operates before field extraction and boolean evaluation occurs — false; both `search` and `where` are search-time commands
`where` filters using eval-style boolean expressions on
`search` and `where` are identical in boolean evaluation capability and syntax — false; `search` uses keyword matching while `where` uses eval-style expressions
`where` works only on non-indexed fields; `search` handles indexed boolean evaluation — partial; `where` works on any field regardless of whether it is indexed
questions.explanation: The `where` command uses eval-style boolean expressions and can reference fields computed by previous pipeline commands. For example, `where length(url) > 200` or `where count > avg_count`. The `search` command in the middle of a pipeline matches against raw event text or explicit field=value pairs but cannot evaluate expressions on computed/aggregated fields. search only matches raw text or field=value pairs

questions.question: A Splunk admin wants to MONITOR a log file (`/var/log/auth.log`) on a Linux host and ship its new lines to the Splunk indexer. The standard mechanism uses a stanza in `inputs.conf` (`[monitor:///var/log/auth.log]`) loaded by a Universal Forwarder or directly on the indexer. Which input type?
options: Scripted input — different (runs a script periodically to monitor and capture stdout; not a file-tailing mechanism)
File monitor input
TCP/UDP input — for syslog / network senders; does not monitor a log file on the local filesystem
HEC (HTTP Event Collector) — REST endpoint for app-pushed events; does not monitor log files on disk
questions.explanation: File monitor inputs use the `[monitor://path]` stanza in `inputs.conf` to tail (continuously read new data from) log files. This is the most common data input method, typically deployed via Universal Forwarder on endpoints. UF watches files and forwards new data to indexers. This differs from scripted inputs (run a script to generate data), TCP/UDP (receive network data), and HEC (HTTP POST).

questions.question: An application team wants to PUSH events to Splunk from a Python microservice without installing a forwarder. They POST JSON payloads to a Splunk-hosted REST endpoint at `https://splunk:8088/services/collector` with a token in the Authorization header. Which Splunk feature?
options: Scheduled API import collector — wrong; HEC is push-based (apps POST to it) rather than Splunk pulling from an external API on a schedule
HTTP Event Collector (HEC)
HTTP access-log collector — different (file monitor tails access logs on disk rather than receiving POSTed events)
Network packet collector — different category (network inspection captures raw packets, not HTTP-posted JSON payloads)
questions.explanation: HTTP Event Collector (HEC) allows applications, scripts, and IoT devices to send events to Splunk via HTTP/HTTPS POST requests using a token-based authentication model — no Universal Forwarder needed. The data is sent as JSON. HEC is ideal for cloud applications, microservices, and scenarios where installing a forwarder is not feasible. scripts, or devices without a forwarder

questions.question: An admin compares two Splunk artefacts. SCHEDULED REPORTS run on a cron schedule + emit results; ALERTS are scheduled reports PLUS a TRIGGER CONDITION (`if number of results > 10 then …`) that fires email / webhook / script. Which describes the difference?
options: Scheduled reports trigger actions when their schedule fires; alerts trigger actions only by email — false; reports can also trigger actions, and alerts support email, webhook, and script actions
Both run on a schedule
Alerts save their schedule results to a CSV; reports display results in dashboards — false; neither is limited to those outputs
Alerts run on a continuous real-time schedule; reports run on a cron schedule — partial (alerts can be real-time OR scheduled; the schedule type is not the defining difference)
questions.explanation: Both scheduled reports and alerts run on a schedule. The key difference is that alerts include trigger conditions that evaluate the search results and only fire an action (email, PagerDuty, run script, etc.) when the condition is met (e.g., number of results > 0). Scheduled reports always run and generate results but don't trigger conditional actions — they are used for generating recurring reports.

questions.question: Splunk's permission ROLES grant capabilities. Default roles: User (search, save in private), POWER USER (create + share knowledge objects in their app), Admin (full system). To allow a knowledge-engineering team to create + share private knowledge objects within their app's permission scope, which role fits?
options: Can Read — read-only, no creation rights; cannot share knowledge objects or create power-user-level constructs
User — can save private knowledge objects, cannot share them in the app scope
Admin — too broad (full system rights including user management); the power user scope is limited to app-level sharing
Power User
questions.explanation: Splunk has three default roles: **User** (can search and save private objects), **Power User** (can create and share knowledge objects app-wide, create alerts, manage lookups — but cannot manage users or global settings), and **Admin** (full system access). Power User is the role target for the Core Certified Power User exam.

questions.question: When sharing a Splunk knowledge object (saved search, dashboard, lookup), the SHARING SCOPE has three levels. (Private) only the creator can see it. (App) visible to all users INSIDE the specific app context (e.g., `search`, `enterprise_security`). (Global) visible across ALL apps to anyone with role permission. Which describes App vs Global?
options: App = visible to all users within the specific app context
App = current user only; Global = all users — false; that's the difference between Private and Global, not App and Global
App = objects stored in the app's specific directory; Global = objects stored in the system directory — partial; directory location follows scope but the question asks about user visibility
App and Global are identical in visibility for Power Users — false; Global makes objects visible across all apps, App restricts visibility to the specific app context
questions.explanation: Knowledge object sharing permissions in Splunk: **Private** = only you, **App** = all users within the same Splunk app context, **Global** = all users in all apps. When sharing a lookup or saved search as 'App', it's available to anyone using that app. 'Global' makes it system-wide. Most Power User objects are shared at the App level. Global: visible across all apps

questions.question: An analyst runs the SPL pipeline `index=web | fields user_agent, status, bytes`. They want to reduce the cost of subsequent commands by carrying forward only the fields they actually need. What does `fields user_agent, status, bytes` do at this position in the pipeline?
options: Restricts the events flowing to subsequent commands to the listed fields plus default internal fields (_time, _raw, etc.) — removing unwanted fields reduces memory and improves subsequent command performance
Filters out events where any of the listed fields is missing or empty before passing them to subsequent commands — field absence filtering uses `where` or `search`, not `fields`
Sorts events by the listed fields in left-to-right order before passing them to subsequent commands in the pipeline — sorting is performed by `sort`, not `fields`
Renames the listed fields to canonical names for subsequent commands — field renaming is performed by `rename`, not `fields`
questions.explanation: The `fields` command controls which fields appear in search results. `fields + field1, field2` includes only those fields (whitelist). `fields - field1, field2` removes those fields from results (blacklist). It is often used to reduce result set size and improve performance by removing unnecessary fields before piping to other commands.

questions.question: A dashboard panel must show event count by sourcetype over the last 24 hours and AUTO-REFRESH every 5 minutes. The team prefers RELATIVE-time historical searches (cheaper) over real-time. Which approach?
options: Real-time 24h panel with a relative-time window — expensive; a real-time search runs continuously against the historical 24h window, which is resource-intensive and often unnecessary
Panels can't auto-refresh their relative-time historical data — false; XML / Studio supports `refresh="5m"` on the panel to rerun the historical search at intervals
Add a relative-time historical search panel with `earliest=-24h` + `latest=now`
Pin a scheduled report to the panel — works but is heavier than using the dashboard's built-in relative-time auto-refresh for a simple historical 24h panel
questions.explanation: Dashboard panels can be configured to auto-refresh at specified intervals (1 min, 5 min, etc.) using the Refresh setting in the panel editor. Setting `earliest=-24h latest=now` with a 5-minute auto-refresh provides a rolling 24-hour view refreshed every 5 minutes. Real-time searches are resource-intensive and generally discouraged for dashboards; scheduled refresh is preferred.

questions.question: An admin defines an EVAL expression in `props.conf` ( `EVAL-response_ms = response_ns / 1000000` ) so that EVERY matching event has the new field at SEARCH TIME — without modifying the raw data or storing the computed value. Which feature?
options: Calculated field
Regex transforms.conf extraction — different mechanism; uses regex patterns rather than an eval expression to extract a field from raw text
Index-time computation — false; calculated fields apply their eval expression at search-time, not at index-time
Stats-based aggregation — different concept; a calculated field computes a per-event value using eval, whereas stats aggregates across multiple events
questions.explanation: A calculated field (Settings > Fields > Calculated Fields) applies an `eval` expression automatically at search time to events of a specific source type. For example, defining `response_kb = bytes / 1024` as a calculated field means it's available in all searches without manually writing `| eval response_kb = bytes / 1024`. It executes at search time, not index time.

questions.question: An ES admin wants to NORMALISE field names across firewall / VPN / endpoint / authentication sources so the same SPL query works regardless of source vendor (e.g., `src_ip` for source IP across Cisco ASA + Palo Alto + Check Point). Splunk publishes a STANDARDISED field-naming convention + data models for this. Which?
options: Compression format — wrong category
ML framework — wrong category
Common Information Model (CIM)
Forwarder protocol — different layer
questions.explanation: The Splunk CIM (Common Information Model) is a shared semantic model provided as an add-on that standardizes field names and data models across different data sources. For example, all authentication data uses `user`, `src`, `dest`, `action` fields regardless of source. CIM enables cross-source searches without knowing vendor-specific field names, and is a prerequisite for apps like Splunk Enterprise Security.

questions.question: A search over 90 days of firewall events with `stats count by src_ip` is slow because it reads raw events. Accelerating the underlying DATA MODEL builds summary indexes. A SPECIFIC SPL command then reads those pre-computed summaries (orders of magnitude faster). Which command?
options: `accelerate` — not a real SPL command (acceleration is configured, not commanded)
`summary` — not a real SPL command
`tstats`
`fast` — not a real SPL command
questions.explanation: The `tstats` command queries accelerated data model summaries or indexed fields (tsidx files) instead of raw events, making it significantly faster for large datasets. It has a different syntax than `stats`: `| tstats count from datamodel=Authentication by Authentication.user`. You must reference fields using the full data model path.

questions.question: An analyst wants to GROUP related events into ONE multi-event transaction (e.g., all events for a single web session sharing `JSESSIONID`, within a 30-min idle gap). The `transaction` command does this but is RESOURCE-EXPENSIVE and should be avoided for high-cardinality / very-long sessions. Which describes `transaction` + the trade-off?
options: ACID-compliant multi-event write transactions — wrong category; SPL `transaction` groups related events for analysis, not database write atomicity
KV-store database transactions that group related records into one atomic write — wrong category; KV Store operations are separate from SPL `transaction` grouping
Multi-step business process orchestration pipelines that group related workflow events — partial; the primary use case is session grouping of related search-time events
Groups related events into one multi-event transaction by a shared field value (e.g., session_id) or a time window, adding `duration` and `eventcount` fields
questions.explanation: The `transaction` command groups related events into a single transaction based on a shared field value (e.g., `session_id`) and optional time/pause constraints. It's useful for tracking session activity or multi-step processes. However, it's memory-intensive and slow for large datasets — `stats` is almost always preferable when the goal is simply aggregation. avoid for large datasets due to high memory usage

questions.question: Two ways to define a field extraction in Splunk: (A) INLINE in `props.conf` using `EXTRACT-<name> = <regex>` — search-time, simple, single file. (B) `TRANSFORMS-<class>` in `props.conf` pointing to a stanza in `transforms.conf` — search-time too, but allows ADDITIONAL features (SOURCE_KEY, format, MV_ADD, REPEAT_MATCH). Which describes the pair?
options: They are identical — both define a simple single-class regex stanza in props.conf that extracts fields at search time with no meaningful difference in features
Inline `EXTRACT-` extracts fields at search time; `TRANSFORMS-class` extracts at index time — false; both can be search-time extractions; only transforms with SOURCE_KEY overrides run at index time

Inline uses `rex` command syntax in the class definition; transforms uses `erex` automatic learning format in the class stanza — false; both use standard regex format in props.conf and transforms.conf

Inline `EXTRACT-name` in props.conf = simple single-stanza regex; `TRANSFORMS-class` in props.conf + transforms.conf stanza = named transforms with features like SOURCE_KEY, FORMAT reuse, and per-sourcetype stanza targeting
questions.explanation: Inline field extractions use `EXTRACT-<name> = <regex>` directly in `props.conf`. Transforms-based extractions define a reusable stanza in `transforms.conf` (with the `REGEX` and `FORMAT` keys) and reference it from `props.conf` with `REPORT-<name> = <transform_stanza_name>`. Transforms are preferred for complex or reusable extractions; inline is simpler for one-off cases. transforms.conf extractions define reusable transform stanzas referenced from props.conf with REPORT-

questions.question: An analyst runs `| makeresults | eval test="hello world" | rex field=test "(?<word>\w+)"`. The single result has `test="hello world"` (2 words). How many ROWS does the final pipeline return, and what's in the captured `word` field?
options: 1 row
2 rows — false; `rex` does NOT split a row per match (use `rex max_match=0` for multi-value capture, but it stays one row)
0 rows — false; rex operates on any field, not just indexed
1 row per captured group — false; row count is input-bound
questions.explanation: By default, `rex` extracts only the **first match** of the pattern from the field. To extract all matches into a multivalue field, use `rex mode=sed` or `rex max_match=0` (which sets no limit). `rex max_match=0 field=test "(?<word>\w+)"` would return a multivalue `word` field containing `["hello", "world"]`.

questions.question: An event has `status=503`. The eval `case(status>=500, "Error", status>=400, "Client Error", status>=200, "Success")` evaluates left-to-right and STOPS at the first true condition. What does `status_label` become?
options: "Success" — wrong; 200 condition matches LAST and is not reached because 500 matches first
"Error"
"Client Error" — wrong; case() stops at the first match
null because multiple conditions match — wrong; case() picks first-match, doesn't return null
questions.explanation: The `case()` function evaluates conditions in order and returns the value for the first matching condition. For status=503: the first condition `status>=500` is true (503 >= 500), so it returns "Error" immediately. The `1=1` at the end is a catch-all that always evaluates to true (like `else`). Conditions are evaluated left to right; first match wins.

questions.question: An analyst wants every event with a `host` field to be ENRICHED at search time with the host's owner + criticality from a KV-store collection `cmdb_hosts`. The enrichment should happen AUTOMATICALLY for the entire app's searches — no need to type `| lookup` each time. Which feature?
options: Automatic lookup pointing to a KV-store collection
Real-time search with subsearch — different mechanism; a subsearch is expensive and requires explicit `| lookup` syntax in SPL rather than automatic store-backed enrichment
Data model acceleration — different; acceleration pre-computes summaries for fast reporting but does not store or deliver per-event enrichment from an external collection
Workflow action — different; a workflow action is a right-click interaction on a field value, not an automatic store-backed enrichment applied to every search
questions.explanation: KV Store lookups work just like CSV lookups but store data in a MongoDB-compatible key-value store. An automatic lookup configured to use a KV Store collection enriches events at search time automatically. KV Store lookups support larger datasets and allow CRUD operations via REST API and Splunk's `outputlookup`/`inputlookup` commands.

questions.question: A search pipeline `| sort -count` orders results by `count` field DESCENDING. The default direction of `sort` (no `+`/`-` prefix) is ASCENDING. Which describes `sort`?
options: Sorts results by _time, newest first by default — `sort` orders by an arbitrary specified field; it is not locked to `_time`
Sorts results by the specified field
Sorts results by a relevance score computed from field frequency — no relevance score concept exists in Splunk SPL `sort`
Sorts results in random order — `random()` does that; `sort` arranges results in ascending or descending field order
questions.explanation: The `sort` command sorts results by one or more fields. The default order is ascending. Use `-` prefix for descending: `sort -count` (highest first). Sort by multiple fields: `sort host, -count` (sort by host ascending, then count descending within each host). `sort 0` removes the default 10,000-result limit on sorted results.

questions.question: From a search result row, an analyst right-clicks the `src_ip` field value and sees a context menu offering 'Open in CMDB', 'Block IP via Firewall API', 'Pivot to ThreatIntel'. These are PRE-CONFIGURED interactive links / form submissions registered against fields or eventtypes. Which knowledge object?
options: Alert escalation workflow — different (alerts framework)
Dashboard publish approval — not a real Splunk feature
Scheduled-report chain — different
Workflow action
questions.explanation: Workflow actions add interactive hyperlinks or POST form submissions to field values in search results. They allow analysts to pivot from a result directly to an external system (e.g., open a WHOIS lookup for an IP, create a JIRA ticket for an event, or run a follow-up Splunk search with a field value pre-filled). They are configured per field per source type. allowing users to pivot to external systems or run follow-up searches

questions.question: An alert fires on every 5-minute schedule whenever the trigger condition is met. The ops team gets spammed with duplicate emails. The admin enables THROTTLING with `suppress for 1 hour by src_ip` — after firing for an IP, the alert won't re-fire for the SAME IP for 1 hour. What does THROTTLE do?
options: Throttle suppresses the alert from firing until a minimum number of trigger events accumulate in the alert results — that is the alert trigger condition threshold, not throttling
Throttle reduces the alert's search schedule frequency so the cron trigger fires less often to lower resource consumption — that is the alert cron schedule setting, not throttling
Throttle limits the number of events returned in the alert results to a fixed count using the same logic as the `head` command — that is result limiting, not alert suppression
Throttle suppresses re-firing of the alert for a specified period (optionally per field value), preventing duplicate notifications when the alert condition persists
questions.explanation: Alert throttling suppresses the alert from firing again for a configurable time window (e.g., 24 hours) after it first triggers, to prevent alert fatigue. You can throttle on a specific field value — for example, throttle for 1 hour per unique `src_ip` so the same attacker IP only triggers one alert per hour instead of one per 5-minute search cycle.

questions.question: A Splunk dashboard exposes a TEXT-INPUT control where users type a hostname. The dashboard panel's search uses `index=main host=$host_input$` — the `$…$` syntax substitutes the user's input. The placeholder is a DASHBOARD-LEVEL variable; updating it re-runs panel searches. Which describes this?
options: Token
HEC token — different (HEC auth, not dashboard variable)
Cached search result — different (job IDs / loadjob)
REST API key — different (auth tokens for API)
questions.explanation: Dashboard tokens (also called tokens) are dynamic variables used in Splunk dashboards. Input controls (dropdowns, text boxes, time pickers) set token values, and panels reference them using `$token_name$` syntax in search strings or panel attributes. This makes dashboards interactive — selecting a value from a dropdown updates all panels that reference that token.

questions.question: A scheduled saved-search computes daily aggregates and PERSISTS the results to a CSV lookup file `daily_totals.csv`. Subsequent dashboards read from the CSV via `| inputlookup daily_totals.csv`. The pipe that WRITES the search's current results into the lookup is `| outputlookup daily_totals.csv`. Which describes `outputlookup`?
options: `inputlookup daily_summary.csv` — reads current records from a CSV lookup file into the search pipeline for joining or enrichment; the opposite direction from `outputlookup` writes
`outputlookup daily_summary.csv` — writes current search results to a CSV lookup file, replacing or appending the file's contents
`outputcsv daily_summary` — writes current search results to a standard CSV export; `outputcsv` is not a valid SPL command for lookup files
`dbxlookup daily_summary` — writes current search results to an external database via a lookup definition; requires the DB Connect app and a different syntax
questions.explanation: `outputlookup` writes search results to a CSV file or KV Store lookup table. This is used to create or update lookup files programmatically. For example, running a daily search that outputs a list of known bad IPs to a CSV, which is then used by `lookup` to enrich future events. Requires write permission on the lookup.

questions.question: A search produces a multivalue field `tags` containing `['prod','db','primary']`. To extract the SECOND element (index 1 — Splunk multivalue indexes are 0-based), the analyst uses an eval function. Which?
options: `mvget(field, idx)` — not a real Splunk eval function
`mvindex(field, 1)`
`getmv(field, idx)` — not a real Splunk function
`field[idx]` — not Splunk SPL syntax
questions.explanation: `mvindex(field, start, end)` extracts a value (or range of values) from a multivalue field by position. Index 0 is the first element, negative indices count from the end (-1 is the last element). For example, `eval last_ip = mvindex(ips, -1)` retrieves the last IP in a multivalue `ips` field. This is commonly used when processing multivalue fields created by `split()`, `mvsort()`, or lookups.

questions.question: An ingest stanza sets no `sourcetype` for the input. How does Splunk DECIDE the sourcetype to assign at index time?
options: Automatic sourcetyping
Universal Forwarder always sets it — false; UF can leave it unset
Inherited from the index — false; index ≠ sourcetype
Always `unknown` — false; only the fallback
questions.explanation: Splunk can automatically detect source types using pattern matching. In `props.conf`, `[source::.../filename.log]` stanzas match by filename pattern. Splunk also has built-in rules for common file types (.csv, .json, Windows event logs, syslog, Apache access logs, etc.). If no rule matches, it falls back to `_json`, `_xml`, or `generic_single_line` based on content analysis.

questions.question: Two ways to JOIN two searches' results: (A) APPENDCOLS — runs a second search and pastes its result COLUMNS side-by-side with the first (matching by row position). (B) APPEND — runs a second search and STACKS its rows below the first (matching by column name). Which describes `appendcols`?
options: Adding new field columns computed from existing fields using `eval` expressions — `eval` generates derived fields side-by-side but does not run a second search or join its columns to the pipeline
Appending rows from a second search below the main results — that is `append`; `appendcols` runs a second search and adds its columns side-by-side rather than stacking rows below
Adding columns from a lookup file side-by-side with events using the `lookup` command — `lookup` enriches events with lookup columns but does not run a second parallel search pipeline
Runs a second search and appends its columns side-by-side with the main results, aligned row-by-row; differs from `append` (adds rows) and `join` (matches on a key field)
questions.explanation: `appendcols` runs a subsearch and appends the columns (fields) from the subsearch results alongside the main search results, row by row. Unlike `append` (which adds rows), `appendcols` adds columns. It's useful for combining two separate aggregations side-by-side. The number of rows in the subsearch should match the main search, or rows are filled with null.

questions.question: A Splunk alert has two scheduling modes. (Real-time) the alert search runs CONTINUOUSLY on a rolling time window (e.g., last 5 min) and trigger conditions are evaluated on every result update — most timely but most resource-heavy. (Scheduled) the alert search runs on a CRON schedule (every N minutes), trigger conditions evaluated after each completion — cheaper but less timely. Which describes Real-time vs Scheduled?
options: Real-time alerts incur heavy overhead but support timely email notifications only; scheduled alerts support all action types — false; both modes support all action types regardless of overhead

Real-time alerts fire every second and are therefore as heavy as scheduled alerts for short intervals — false; the rolling window length is configurable and real-time evaluation is heavier than scheduled

Real-time alerts use streaming-only evaluation on new events; scheduled alerts search historical data only — false; both modes can search live or historical data depending on the configured time window
Real-time = continuous rolling-window evaluation (most timely, resource-heavy)
questions.explanation: Real-time alerts in Splunk continuously evaluate a rolling time window (e.g., always looking at the last 5 minutes of data). The trigger condition is checked as new events arrive. Scheduled alerts run the search at specific intervals (every 15 minutes, hourly, etc.) and check results at that point in time. Real-time alerts are resource-intensive and generally reserved for high-priority use cases. Scheduled runs the search at defined intervals

questions.question: An analyst wants to enrich firewall events with user-email by JOINING to an LDAP-backed lookup. Splunk's `join` command does it but is RESOURCE-HEAVY (loads both result sets into memory) and has a default 50 000-row cap. A more efficient alternative is `stats` with `by` clauses or a lookup. What does `join` do?
options: `join field=key …`
Combines multivalue field values into a single joined string — that's `mvjoin`, not the SQL-style `join` command
The `join` command was deprecated in Splunk 8.x for field-based enrichment — false; `join` is still supported in current versions
Connects to an external database using a field key to retrieve matching rows — that requires the DB Connect app; SPL `join` operates on subsearch results only
questions.explanation: The `join` command performs a SQL-style join between the main search results and a subsearch on a shared field. It's functionally correct but slow on large datasets. Better alternatives: use `lookup` for enrichment from reference tables (much faster), `stats` for aggregation-based joins, or `append + stats` for union-style operations. Avoid `join` in performance-sensitive searches. subsearch or lookup are usually better alternatives for performance

questions.question: Splunk time modifier `earliest=-60m@m latest=@m` snaps both bounds to the START of a minute. So `-60m@m` means 60 minutes ago snapped down to that minute's :00 seconds; `@m` means the current minute's :00 seconds. Effective range = the previous 60 minutes (start-of-minute aligned). Which describes this?
options: Last full hour with hour-snap — false; `@m` snaps to the minute boundary, not the hour; hour-snapping would use `@h`, e.g., `earliest=-1h@h`
From 60 minutes ago to now with no snapping — partially correct on the offset but ignores the `@m` snap-to-minute boundary on both bounds
From 60 minutes ago snapped to the start of that day's midnight to the current day's midnight — wrong unit; `@m` snaps to the minute boundary, not `@d` for day
From 60 minutes ago snapped to that minute's start to the current minute's start
questions.explanation: `earliest=-60m@m` means 60 minutes ago, then snap back to the start of that minute (i.e., the minute boundary 60 minutes ago). `latest=@m` means the start of the current minute. Together this gives you a clean rolling 60-minute window aligned to minute boundaries, useful for reporting where you don't want partial minutes at the edges.

questions.question: A reporting team needs 3 years of MONTHLY firewall-event aggregates without storing 3 years of raw events. They schedule a search every night that AGGREGATES the day's events with `stats count by …` and writes the SUMMARY ROWS to a dedicated index (e.g., `summary`). Dashboards query the summary index → fast. Which technique?
options: Summary indexing
Main index aggregation — wrong; the main index is the live data store for raw events, not a summary destination
Alert-history index — wrong purpose; alert history tracks fired alert records, not pre-aggregated summary rows
Field-stats index — not a real Splunk index; summary rows are written to a dedicated summary index using the `collect` command
questions.explanation: Summary indexing writes aggregated results (e.g., hourly counts, daily totals) to a separate Splunk index using `collect` or `sichart`/`sistats` commands. This allows very fast querying of long-term trends by searching pre-aggregated data instead of raw events, dramatically reducing search time and resource consumption for reporting on months of data.

questions.question: An event has `tags="prod,db,primary"` as a STRING. To convert it into a Splunk multivalue field so per-element commands (`mvexpand`, `mvindex`) work, the analyst splits the string on comma. Which SPL idiom?
options: `| makemv field delim=","` — VALID (makemv) but the eval-based approach is more general
`| eval tags = split(tags, ",")`
`| fields split(tags, ",")` — wrong; `fields` doesn't run functions
`| mvexpand tags delimiter=","` — wrong syntax; `mvexpand` expects an already-multivalue field
questions.explanation: The `eval split(field, delimiter)` function splits a string into a multivalue field using the specified delimiter. `eval apps = split(app_list, ",")` creates a multivalue `apps` field from a comma-separated string. The `makemv` command (also correct for some formats) is used for fields that are already stored as multivalue strings with a delimiter.

questions.question: An event has a multivalue field `users = ['alice','bob','carol']`. The analyst wants ONE row per user (3 rows total) so they can `stats` per user. Which SPL command?
options: `mvexpand users`
Splits a single event into multiple by delimiter — that's `split` (eval) followed by `mvexpand`
Expands macro variables — wrong command (that's macro substitution at parse time)
Expands data-model summary — different concept
questions.explanation: `mvexpand` takes a multivalue field and creates a separate event for each value in that field. For example, if an event has `ports=[80, 443, 8080]`, `| mvexpand ports` creates three events — one for each port value. This is the inverse of `stats values()` — useful for un-grouping multivalue data for further processing.

questions.question: Splunk's data model knowledge object is a HIERARCHICAL definition of: ROOT EVENT (a base search defining the dataset), CHILD events / transactions (filtered subsets), CONSTRAINTS (`eval`, `lookup`, calculated fields per dataset). Used by pivot reports + accelerated by tstats. Which describes a data model?
options: A visual schema builder defining a hierarchical search tree of root event and child event components for accelerated pivot reports — data models are a knowledge object, not a visualisation builder; this misrepresents the structure
A hierarchical knowledge object defining datasets as root event, child event, transaction, and search types, enabling accelerated pivot reports and CIM-compliant field naming
A CIM extension pack only — CIM ships pre-built data models but defining a hierarchical child event and search type structure is not limited to the CIM domain

A configuration file defining hierarchical stanzas that map root event and child event patterns to Splunk indexes via a search constraint — that is `inputs.conf` and `transforms.conf`; data models are search-time knowledge objects, not ingest configs
questions.explanation: A data model is a hierarchical knowledge object that organizes data into structured datasets (event-based, search-based, or transaction-based). Root datasets define the top-level search constraint; child datasets inherit and add constraints. Each dataset has defined fields (attributes). Data models can be accelerated (stored as TSIDX files) for fast `tstats` queries. The CIM ships several pre-built data models. components are root datasets, child datasets, and field definitions

questions.question: An analyst needs RUNNING / CUMULATIVE statistics as events flow through the pipeline in time order: e.g., 'running sum of bytes per host'. `stats` produces ONE row per group (collapses events); the streaming alternative keeps each event AND adds a new field with the running aggregate. Which command?
options: `streamstats sum(bytes) AS running_bytes BY host`

Uses streaming algorithms at the implementation level, computing running aggregates in a bytes-efficient single pass — true at the implementation level but not the user-facing distinction from `stats`
Produces running aggregates faster than `stats` because it skips bytes of intermediate data — context-dependent; performance advantage is not universal
Computes running aggregates for real-time searches only, tracking bytes per host as events stream in — false; `streamstats` works on historical searches too
questions.explanation: `streamstats` computes statistics in a running/cumulative fashion, adding the stat as a field to each event — the result still has the same number of rows as the input. For example, `streamstats sum(bytes) as cumulative_bytes by session_id` adds a running byte total per session to each event. `stats` collapses all events into a summary table. `streamstats` is ideal for detecting rate changes or running totals. adding stats fields to each event without collapsing results into a summary table

questions.question: Splunk extracts fields in TWO architectural stages. (A) INDEX-TIME — fields stored alongside raw event in the index; reading the field doesn't require regex execution; FASTER searches but BIGGER index storage. (B) SEARCH-TIME — fields extracted at query time via regex / delimiter; ZERO storage cost but per-query CPU. Which describes the trade-off?
options: Index-time uses regex to extract field values for faster access; search-time uses key=value pair parsing only — false; both index-time and search-time extractions use regex defined in props.conf

The distinction is just documentation terminology with no architectural difference; both approaches achieve equally faster field retrieval with the same storage impact — false; index-time stores values in the index for faster searches at the cost of larger storage
Index-time stores field values in the index (faster search, larger

Index-time field extraction handles structured data for faster lookups; search-time handles unstructured data with no speed advantage — partial; both can apply to any data format; the difference is when extraction runs
questions.explanation: Splunk recommends search-time field extraction for almost all use cases. **Index-time** extraction permanently writes field values into the index (increasing storage) — only use for fields needed in very high-performance searches. **Search-time** extraction happens when a search runs, extracting fields from the raw `_raw` text on the fly using regex defined in `props.conf`. This is flexible and storage-efficient. search-time extraction happens on-the-fly when a search is run

questions.question: An analyst searches for HTTP requests where the URL contains `/admin`. The MOST efficient SPL pattern uses indexed-field matching with a wildcard (lets Splunk push the search to the indexer's lispy engine, NOT post-process via `where`/`regex`). Which?
options: `index=web url=*admin*`
`| eval match=if(match(url,"/admin"),1,0) | where match=1` — post-process every event; far slower
`| search url=*admin*` — works but the leading `index=web` already supports it inline; same engine path
`| regex url="/admin"` — works but `regex` is post-process and slower than indexed wildcard match
questions.explanation: Placing `url=*admin*` directly in the main search string (before the first pipe) uses index-aware optimization and can narrow the event set using bloom filters and bucket elimination where possible. Using `search` after a pipe, `regex`, or `eval/where` all operate on the full result set after the initial retrieval. Note that wildcard-only searches (`*admin*`) still scan raw events but are faster than post-pipe filtering for initial event reduction.

questions.question: An analyst has events with continuous numeric `response_ms` ranging 0-5000. They want to bucket events into ranges (`0-99`, `100-499`, `500-999`, `1000+`) for histogram visualization. The SPL command that DISCRETISES continuous numeric (or time) fields into buckets is `bin` (alias `bucket`). Which describes `bin`?
options: Marks events for deletion based on the span value of a response field — wrong; `bin` discretises values, it does not delete events
`bin span=100 response_ms`
Distributes search work across indexer buckets based on the response field span — wrong; indexer buckets are a storage concept unrelated to the `bin` command
Compresses the response field to a binary representation for faster span-based queries — wrong; `bin` groups numeric values into ranges, not a compression operation
questions.explanation: `bin` (alias: `bucket`) groups continuous field values into discrete ranges for aggregation. Common use: `bin _time span=1h` creates hourly time buckets for use with `stats`. Example: `bin bytes span=1024` creates 1KB buckets. After `bin`, use `stats count by` the binned field to get histograms. `timechart` uses `bin` internally on `_time`.

questions.question: Which is a valid Splunk SPL `eval if(...)` form? Splunk's `if(cond, true_val, false_val)` is COMMA-SEPARATED, NOT keyword-based, and uses `==` for equality comparison.
options: `if(status=200) then "OK" else "Not OK"` — wrong cond syntax; Splunk `if()` uses comma-separated arguments (cond, true_val, false_val) not then/else keyword syntax
`case(status=200, "OK", true(), "Not OK")` — this is the `case()` function which evaluates each cond in order, not `if()`; also uses `=` instead of the required `==`
`if(status==200, "OK", "Not OK")` — canonical eval if: comma-separated (cond, true, false); use `==` for equality
`if(status=200, "OK", "Not OK")` — the `=` operator is assignment, not a cond operator; equality comparison in Splunk eval requires `==`
questions.explanation: In Splunk `eval`, the `if()` function uses comparison operators: `==` for equality, `!=` for not equal, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`. The syntax is `if(condition, true_value, false_value)`. Note that in the `search` command you use single `=` for field matching, but in `eval` expressions you must use `==` for equality comparison. Option A would cause an error in eval context.

questions.question: Two SPL commands to select fields. (A) `fields` — includes / excludes fields from the pipeline but does NOT guarantee column ORDER in the final output. (B) `table` — selects fields AND preserves the specified COLUMN ORDER in the final result table. Which describes the difference?
options: `table` is a visualisation layer that renders the specified fields; `fields` is a pipeline command — false; both are pipeline commands that control which fields appear in the output, not visualisation layers
`table` and `fields` produce identical formatted output for the specified column list — false; `table` enforces the specified column order while `fields` does not guarantee column order
`table` creates a FORMATTED table preserving the specified column order (and

The only difference is execution location: `table` runs on the search head for the specified fields; `fields` runs on indexers — partial; the user-facing difference is column-order behaviour, not execution location
questions.explanation: `table` is a transforming command that creates a table displaying only the specified fields in the specified column order. `fields` is a streaming command that includes or excludes fields but doesn't control display order. `table field1, field2, field3` both selects fields AND defines their left-to-right order in the results table. `table` converts the output to a structured table view, consuming results. fields includes/excludes fields but doesn't define column order

questions.question: Splunk supports REPORT ACCELERATION: a saved REPORT (search) is registered for acceleration, and Splunk PRE-COMPUTES summaries for that report's time range (every 10 min by default). Subsequent runs of the SAME report read the summaries — orders-of-magnitude faster than re-running raw. Which describes report acceleration?
options: In-memory cache that pre-computes summaries for a saved report in RAM — false; report acceleration stores pre-computed summaries as files on disk, not in RAM
Pre-computes summaries for a saved report
Native-code compilation that pre-computes summaries for a saved report into a binary format — false; acceleration uses summary indexing, not native-code compilation

Distributes the saved report's pre-computed summaries across all indexers for parallel retrieval — partial; acceleration runs on indexers but it operates by writing local summary files, not distributing pre-computed data across nodes
questions.explanation: Report acceleration pre-builds summaries for a saved report by running it continuously in the background, storing partial results that speed up future runs. Requirements: (1) the report must contain transforming commands, (2) it should run regularly (daily or more frequent), and (3) acceleration must be enabled in the report settings. The acceleration summaries are stored separately from the main index. requires the report to use transforming commands and to be on a regular schedule

questions.question: An analyst runs `| lookup customers customer_id AS user_id OUTPUT name` but gets ZERO matched rows even though the CSV has matching entries. The CSV has a column `customer_id` and events have `user_id`. Most likely cause?
options: The CSV lookup file was modified externally and its customer_id column header was changed, so the output field name mapping no longer takes effect — partially true in some cases but the primary cause here is a field name mismatch between the lookup definition and the event field

The lookup's input field name in the lookup definition (`customer_id`) doesn't match the event field name (`user_id`) — using `AS user_id` aliases the event field but the lookup definition still expects `customer_id` as the output key

CSV lookups cannot perform case-sensitive customer_id name matching, so rows whose `name` output values contain mixed case are silently dropped — case-sensitivity is configurable in the lookup definition and is not the cause of zero matches here

The lookup file is too large and was truncated during upload, dropping all rows that contain the customer_id and `name` output fields — the zero-match symptom here is a field name mismatch, not file truncation
questions.explanation: The most common cause of lookup returning 0 enrichment results is a mismatch between the input field name in the lookup definition and the field name that actually exists in the events. For example, if the lookup definition specifies input field `src_ip` but events have the field as `src`, the lookup won't find matches. Check the field name exactly. Case sensitivity of values is the second most common issue (default lookups are case-sensitive).

questions.question: An analyst wants to PLOT geo-distributed events on a Splunk choropleth (region) map or cluster (lat/lng) map. The data has src_ip → geo lat/lng (via iplocation). The command that aggregates events into the lat/lng grid format consumed by map visualisations is `geostats`. Which?
options: Extracts geo from IP — that's `iplocation`
Calculates distances — wrong concept
Generates aggregated stats SUITABLE FOR MAPPING on
Statistical significance of geo trends — different concept
questions.explanation: `geostats` is a transforming command that generates statistics for geographic map visualizations. It aggregates data by latitude/longitude coordinates into grid cells at the appropriate zoom level. It requires latitude and longitude fields (often derived from iplocation). The output feeds Splunk's map visualization for plotting density or counts geographically. Example: `iplocation src_ip | geostats count by action`.

questions.question: An analyst wants to compute `avg(response_ms) BY host` but KEEP EACH ORIGINAL EVENT AND add the per-host average as a new field on each event (so they can compare each event to the host average). `stats` collapses to one row per host. The streaming alternative preserves events. Which command?
options: `eventstats avg(response_ms) AS avg_by_host BY host` — computes avg(response_ms) per host and appends it as a new field to each original event without removing any events

Use `eventstats` to search across multiple indexes simultaneously; each event from every index gets avg(response_ms) appended as a field — false; `eventstats` operates on the current pipeline results, not across multiple indexes

Use `eventstats` for aggregation functions that `stats` doesn't support, such as computing a running average for each event — false; both commands support the same function set; the key difference is that `eventstats` preserves original events while `stats` collapses them

Use `eventstats` for real-time searches only, since each event must be evaluated in streaming mode to append avg(response_ms) per host — false; `eventstats` works on both historical and real-time searches
questions.explanation: `eventstats` computes aggregate statistics and adds them as new fields to every original event — the result has the same number of rows as the input. `stats` collapses all events into a summary table. Example: `eventstats avg(bytes) as avg_bytes` adds the overall average as a field to each event, allowing `where bytes > avg_bytes` to filter above-average events. This pattern is very common in security analytics.

questions.question: Which TWO SPL search commands are STREAMING (can be distributed to indexers and run before the search head sees the data)?
options: eval
stats
rex
sort
questions.explanation: `eval` and `rex` operate on each event independently — they're streaming and run on the indexers in a distributed search. `stats` and `sort` are transforming commands that need to see all results, so they run on the search head after data is gathered.
